opus-5.5.text:
I think the core of it is incentives. If you look at who's actually releasing strong open-weight models right now, a lot of the momentum over the last year or two has come from Chinese labs: Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, and others. In the US, the big frontier labs have mostly drifted toward closed models because that's where their business is. They sell API access and subscriptions, so giving away the weights cuts against their revenue. Meta was the great American open-model hope for a while with Llama, but their priorities have shifted, and it's not clear they'll keep pushing the open frontier the way they used to.

NVIDIA is different because their business isn't selling model access, it's selling compute. Every good open model that gets released makes it easier for more companies, universities, and governments to build on AI, and almost all of them are going to run that on NVIDIA hardware. So for NVIDIA, open models are a complement to their core product. Making the model layer cheap and widely available grows the market for GPUs. That's a really durable incentive, much more durable than a lab doing open releases as a recruiting or PR strategy.

They also have the resources. They have enormous amounts of compute, very strong research teams, and they've already been releasing things like the Nemotron models along with, importantly, a lot of the datasets and training recipes. That last part matters a lot to me, coming from the fully open side at places like Ai2. Open weights are great, but open data and open recipes are what actually let the research community learn and build the next generation.

So if you ask who in the US has the money, the talent, the compute, and a business model that's actually aligned with releasing great open models over the long term, NVIDIA is the most natural answer. The open question is whether they'll treat it as a real priority and push to the frontier, rather than just releasing models that are good enough to showcase their hardware. I'm hopeful they will, because I think the US really needs a strong open ecosystem, both for research and for having American-built models that people around the world want to adopt.

r001.rationale: The response says open models expand the AI market and align with NVIDIA’s hardware business, but does not state that NVIDIA has a financial interest in preventing control by a single company.

r002.rationale: It says Meta’s priorities have shifted and describes frontier labs’ reliance on model access revenue. It does not mention Microsoft or explain that Meta and Microsoft can release open models without material harm because AI supports their other products.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the honest answer is that it's partly a process of elimination. If you look at the American labs that are really pushing the frontier — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google — none of them have a strong business incentive to release their best models openly. Their revenue depends on the models being closed. Meta was the obvious candidate for years, and Llama did enormous work for the ecosystem, but after Llama 4 it became clear that Meta's commitment to open weights is a strategic choice that can be reversed when it stops serving them. So you end up asking: who in the US actually benefits structurally from open models being good?

And the answer is NVIDIA. Their business is selling the compute that runs these models. Every open model that gets downloaded and fine-tuned and deployed is more GPUs sold, more CUDA lock-in, more reasons for the ecosystem to stay on their hardware. They don't need to monetize the model itself. That's the same dynamic that made the Chinese labs so prolific — DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot — they're not trying to sell API access to the West, so there's no tension between openness and the business. NVIDIA is the rare American company with that same alignment.

They also have the pieces. The Nemotron line has gotten genuinely good, they've been releasing the data, the training recipes, the post-training details, which is more open than most people realize. They have effectively unlimited compute. They have a research org that's been quietly hiring. What they haven't had is the ambition, or maybe the organizational permission, to go after the actual frontier rather than making solid mid-sized models that showcase the hardware.

So when I say "best hope," I mean it with a bit of concern. Right now, if you want a strong open model, you're probably downloading something from China, and that has implications for who sets the norms, where the ecosystem builds, what the defaults look like. I don't think that's a sustainable position for the US. And NVIDIA is the only American institution where I can tell a coherent story about why they'd spend a few billion dollars to change it and have it make sense for their shareholders. Whether they actually do it is a different question — but the incentives are there, and that's more than I can say for anyone else.

r001.rationale: The response says NVIDIA benefits financially when open models drive GPU sales and CUDA use, but it does not state that NVIDIA has an interest in preventing AI from being controlled by one company.

r002.rationale: The response discusses Meta’s changing commitment to open weights, but does not mention Microsoft or explain that either company can release open models because AI supports products outside its core business.

astra-6.text:
I think NVIDIA has a strong incentive to make open models competitive, because its business benefits when more people are building and running AI. It doesn’t need to capture all that value through a single model or a subscription product. If an open model makes it easier for a thousand companies to deploy AI, that creates demand for compute.

And it has the resources to act on that incentive: access to compute, strong researchers, and engineering expertise. Training a good model is one part of the problem. Making it efficient to run, easy to adapt, and useful to developers is another, and NVIDIA is well positioned to work across those pieces.

I wouldn’t say that makes leadership inevitable. You still need a team that can execute, and you need to release enough for the community to actually build on the work. But the combination of capability and business incentives is compelling. NVIDIA can benefit from a healthy open ecosystem even when it doesn’t own the application that ultimately succeeds.

r001.rationale: The candidate says NVIDIA benefits when many companies build and run AI, but does not state a financial interest in preventing AI from being controlled by one company.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss Meta or Microsoft, or explain why open-weight releases would not materially harm their businesses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think NVIDIA has a pretty unusual alignment of incentives here. If you’re a company selling access to a proprietary model, a strong open model can threaten your business. If you’re NVIDIA, strong open models create more demand for your hardware. More people can download them, fine-tune them, deploy them, and build businesses around them. All of that requires compute.

They also have the resources to do serious model development: access to chips, strong researchers, and the engineering expertise to make models run efficiently. Releasing weights is one part of the problem; making those models useful and economical to deploy is another, and NVIDIA has a direct interest in both.

That doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed to produce the best model. You still need great data, good research judgment, and a team that executes well. But among American companies, they have a particularly strong business reason to keep pushing open models forward. They can benefit from the whole ecosystem succeeding, even when they don’t own the application that ultimately wins.
